title: The Human Body · Episode 2
chapters: Your teeth: the hardest part of you
Your microbiome: the trillions living inside you

units.t: The Human Body. Episode two.
In this episode: How your voice works, Your teeth: the hardest part of you, How digestion works and Your microbiome: the trillions living inside you.
Part one. How your voice works.
Every word you speak begins as a buzz from two tiny folds of tissue in your throat.
The rest is shaped by your body like a musical instrument.
The voice box.
Sitting at the top of your windpipe is the larynx, or voice box, a structure of cartilage, muscle and ligament.
The bump at the front of the neck, the Adam's apple, is part of its largest cartilage and tends to stick out more in men.
Stretched across the airway are two vocal folds.
They are often called vocal cords, but they are not strings.
Each is a layered band of muscle and ligament covered in soft, moist membrane.
When you breathe, the folds swing apart to let air through.
When you swallow, they snap shut, helping stop food and drink going down the wrong way.
When you speak, they come together and vibrate.
Making the buzz.
To make sound, muscles bring the vocal folds together.
Air pushed up from the lungs builds pressure beneath them until it forces them apart and a puff escapes.
The folds spring back together, helped by their own elasticity and the pressure drop as air rushes between them, and the cycle repeats.
It happens remarkably fast.
A typical adult man's speaking voice vibrates at around 100 to 120 cycles per second, and a typical woman's at around 200.
Tighter, thinner folds vibrate faster and make higher notes, which is how you change pitch.
Push more air through and the sound gets louder.
On its own, though, this buzz sounds nothing like speech.
Shaping the sound.
The raw buzz travels up through the throat, mouth and nose, which together form the vocal tract.
Like a guitar's body, this space strengthens some frequencies and weakens others.
By moving your tongue, lips, jaw and soft palate you change its shape, and with it the sound.
Vowels depend mainly on tongue and lip position: say "ee" then "oo" and feel the difference.
Consonants come from briefly blocking or narrowing airflow with the lips, teeth or tongue.
Whispering shows the two systems working separately.
Your vocal folds do not vibrate at all, yet you still form clear words using the air rushing through your mouth.
Why voices change.
Children of both sexes have similar voices because their larynxes are similar in size.
At puberty, testosterone makes the larynx grow and the vocal folds lengthen and thicken, especially in boys.
Longer, heavier folds vibrate more slowly, and many male voices drop by around an octave.
During the change a voice may crack unpredictably as the muscles adjust to a rapidly changing instrument.
Girls' voices deepen too, but only slightly.
Voices keep changing throughout life.
In older age, vocal folds can thin and lose some muscle, making a voice weaker or breathier.
Hormonal changes around menopause can also lower a woman's voice a little.
Hearing and caring for it.
Most people wince at a recording of their own voice.
Others hear you only through the air, but you also hear yourself through the bones of your skull.
Bone conduction carries low frequencies well, so the voice in your head sounds deeper and fuller.
A recording captures only the airborne version, which is closer to what others hear.
Because the folds collide many times a second, heavy use takes a toll.
Teachers, singers, coaches and call centre workers are most at risk of voice problems, including swelling or small callus-like growths called vocal nodules.
Rest a sore voice, avoid habitual shouting, stay hydrated and do not smoke.
Whispering is not necessarily restful.
Hoarseness from a cold usually settles within a week or two, but if it lasts more than about three weeks, see a doctor.
The key idea: Your voice is made in the larynx, where two vocal folds sit across the airway and vibrate when you speak.
Part two. Your teeth: the hardest part of you.
Your teeth are coated in the toughest material your body makes, yet a bag of lollies can slowly dissolve it.
Here is how they work and how to keep them.
Built in layers.
A tooth is built like a fortress.
The outer layer of the crown is enamel, the hardest substance in the human body.
It is about 96 per cent mineral, mostly crystals of a calcium phosphate called hydroxyapatite.
Beneath it lies dentine, softer and full of microscopic tubes, which is why a worn or cracked tooth can feel sensitive to cold.
At the centre is the pulp, a soft core of nerves and blood vessels that keeps the tooth alive.
Tiny fibres called the periodontal ligament anchor the root into the jawbone.
Enamel has one great weakness: it contains no living cells, so once it is lost the body cannot grow it back.
Two sets for life.
Like most mammals, we get two sets of teeth.
Children have 20 baby teeth, which usually start appearing at around six months, while the adult teeth are already forming deep in the jaw.
From about age six the baby teeth loosen and fall out as permanent teeth push up from below.
A full adult set has 32 teeth: incisors for cutting, canines for tearing, premolars and molars for grinding.
The last four molars, the wisdom teeth, usually arrive between the late teens and mid twenties, if they arrive at all.
Unlike sharks, which replace teeth throughout their lives, we get no third set.
How decay happens.
Your mouth is home to hundreds of species of bacteria, living in a sticky film called plaque.
Some, including Streptococcus mutans, feed on sugars and release acid as waste.
When a tooth surface becomes acidic enough, roughly below a pH of 5.
5, minerals begin to dissolve out of the enamel.
Saliva fights back.
It neutralises acid and supplies calcium and phosphate that can rebuild early damage.
Trouble starts when attacks come too often for saliva to keep up.
That is why how often you eat sugar matters more than the total amount.
Sipping soft drink all afternoon is harder on teeth than having one with lunch.
The brown stain mystery.
In the early 1900s a young dentist named Frederick McKay moved to Colorado Springs and noticed many locals had brown-stained teeth.
Over years he found those teeth were strangely resistant to decay, and the cause was eventually traced to naturally high fluoride in the water.
Researchers then worked out that a much lower level could reduce decay without staining.
In 1945 Grand Rapids, Michigan, became the first city to add fluoride to its water deliberately.
In Australia, the Tasmanian town of Beaconsfield led the way in 1953.
Fluoride helps enamel rebuild into a form called fluorapatite, which resists acid better than the original.
Gums and daily care.
Healthy teeth can still be lost if the gums and bone fail.
Plaque left along the gumline causes gingivitis: redness, swelling and bleeding when you brush.
At this stage good cleaning reverses it.
Left in place, plaque hardens into tartar, which a toothbrush cannot remove.
Ongoing inflammation can progress to periodontitis, where pockets form and the supporting bone is gradually destroyed, so teeth loosen and may fall out.
Gum disease has been linked with diabetes and heart disease, though how much one causes the other is still studied.
People have cleaned teeth for thousands of years, from chew sticks to hog-hair brushes, and nylon bristles arrived in 1938.
Australian dental authorities recommend brushing twice a day with fluoride toothpaste, cleaning between teeth, and spitting rather than rinsing so some fluoride stays on the enamel.
The key idea: Enamel is the hardest substance in the body, but it has no living cells, so lost enamel cannot regrow.
Part three. How digestion works.
From first bite to final exit, your food travels through several metres of tubing and takes a day or more.
Here's what happens along the way.
Mouth to stomach.
The digestive tract is a long tube from mouth to anus, often quoted as about nine metres in an adult.
Chewing breaks food up, and saliva, about half a litre to one and a half litres a day, contains amylase, which starts turning starch into sugar.
That's why bread tastes slightly sweet if chewed long enough.
Waves of muscle contraction, called peristalsis, push food down the oesophagus, even if you're upside down.
The stomach is a stretchy muscular bag that churns food with hydrochloric acid, which kills many microbes, and pepsin, which starts digesting protein.
Mucus protects its lining, which renews every few days.
After a few hours, the thick liquid called chyme is released gradually into the small intestine.
The small intestine.
Despite its name, the small intestine is the longest part of the tract, several metres long and a few centimetres wide.
Bile from the liver breaks fat into droplets, and pancreatic enzymes break down carbohydrates, proteins and fats into sugars, amino acids and fatty acids.
Millions of finger-like villi, covered in even smaller microvilli, give a huge surface area to absorb nutrients into the blood.
Blood from the gut goes first to the liver, which processes nutrients, stores energy as glycogen and removes toxins, including alcohol.
The largest internal organ, it can regenerate remarkably.
The pancreas also makes insulin, which helps cells absorb sugar.
The large intestine.
What's left, mostly fibre, water and bacteria, passes into the large intestine, or colon, about 1.
5 metres long.
Here water and salts are absorbed, turning liquid waste into solid stool, which can take a day or more.
The colon is home to trillions of bacteria, the gut microbiome.
They ferment fibre, produce some vitamins such as vitamin K, and help train the immune system.
Fermenting fibre also makes short-chain fatty acids that help nourish the colon lining.
Researchers are actively studying links between the microbiome and health, though many popular claims go beyond current evidence.
Hunger and fullness.
Your gut and brain talk constantly, through hormones and the vagus nerve.
An empty stomach releases ghrelin, which increases hunger.
As you eat, the stomach stretches and the intestine releases hormones that signal fullness.
Fat tissue releases leptin, which helps regulate appetite over the longer term.
These signals take time to register, which is one reason eating quickly makes it easier to overeat.
Short sleep and stress also affect appetite; short sleep, for example, is linked to stronger hunger.
The gut even has its own vast network of nerves, sometimes called the second brain.
When things go wrong.
Reflux, where acid flows back into the oesophagus, causes heartburn; large meals, lying down after eating and alcohol worsen it.
Many adults make less lactase after childhood, so dairy may cause bloating.
Coeliac disease, an immune reaction to gluten, affects roughly 1 in 70 Australians, and most don't know they have it.
Irritable bowel syndrome causes pain and changed bowel habits without visible damage.
Symptoms overlap, so see a GP rather than cutting out foods on your own.
Most Australians eat less fibre than recommended.
Vegetables, fruit, legumes and whole grains keep you regular and feed healthy bacteria.
Seek advice about persistent bowel changes, blood in stool or unexplained weight loss.
Free bowel cancer screening kits are available from age 45.
The key idea: Digestion starts with chewing and saliva, then the stomach churns food with acid.
Part four. Your microbiome: the trillions living inside you.
You are not just you.
Your gut is home to a vast, bustling community of microbes that digest food you cannot, train your immune system and may even chat with your brain.
An inner rainforest.
Your large intestine is like a rainforest: warm, dark and teeming.
It hosts trillions of microorganisms, mostly bacteria, along with archaea, fungi and viruses.
Together they are the gut microbiota, and their combined genes are the microbiome.
Hundreds of species may live in one gut, in a mix so individual it is compared to a fingerprint.
Most are long-term residents that are helpful or harmless, weighing perhaps a couple of hundred grams, about a mango.
For decades, people repeated that microbes outnumber human cells ten to one, based on a rough 1970s estimate.
In 2016, researchers recalculated it as closer to one to one, with tens of trillions of each.
Catchy statistics can outlive their evidence.
Eating what you cannot.
We lack the enzymes to break down many types of dietary fibre, such as those in legumes, oats, wholegrains, vegetables and fruit.
That fibre reaches the large intestine largely intact, where microbes ferment it.
This produces gases, which explains the noisy consequences of a big serve of baked beans, and short-chain fatty acids.
One of these, butyrate, is a key fuel for the cells lining the colon.
Short-chain fatty acids also appear to influence inflammation and metabolism elsewhere in the body.
Gut bacteria help make some vitamins too, including vitamin K. In a real sense, eating fibre is a way of feeding the microbes that help feed you.
Immunity and a first gift.
A baby's gut is thought to be largely free of microbes before birth.
Colonisation begins during and after delivery, from the mother, the environment and early feeding.
Vaginal and caesarean births tend to start with different communities, though the differences seem to narrow over time.
Breast milk contains sugars the baby cannot digest but certain beneficial bacteria can.
Much of the body's immune tissue sits along the gut.
Germ-free laboratory animals develop abnormal immune systems, suggesting microbes help train it.
A diverse community also provides colonisation resistance: it takes up space and resources, making it harder for harmful bacteria to settle in.
The microbiome becomes adult-like within a few years, then keeps responding to diet, illness, travel, medicines and age.
Transplants and the brain.
The most dramatic proof that gut microbes matter is faecal microbiota transplantation.

It sounds unappealing, but for people with recurring Clostridioides difficile infections, often triggered by antibiotics, screened stool from a healthy donor can restore a healthy community and has proved remarkably effective.
Researchers are also exploring the gut-brain axis, the network of nerves, hormones and immune signals linking gut and brain.
Animal studies suggest microbes can influence behaviour and mood, and human studies have found associations with various conditions.
But association is not cause, and much of this work is early.
Be wary of headlines claiming a particular bacterium causes or cures complex conditions.
The science is fascinating, but still unfolding.
Caring for your microbes.
The best-supported advice is not exotic.
Eat a wide variety of plant foods, such as vegetables, fruit, legumes, wholegrains, nuts and seeds, to provide the range of fibres that different microbes thrive on.
Fermented foods such as yoghurt, kefir and kimchi contain live microbes and may increase diversity, though more research is needed.
Probiotic supplements vary greatly in evidence depending on the strain and condition, and many claims run ahead of the science.
Antibiotics are life-saving when needed, but they can kill helpful bacteria and sometimes cause diarrhoea, so use them only when appropriate.
This is general information, not medical advice.
Talk with your GP or an accredited practising dietitian about specific gut concerns.
The key idea: Your gut hosts trillions of microbes, and the old claim that they outnumber your cells ten to one is wrong.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. What do the vocal folds do when you swallow?
Answer. Close to help protect the airway.
Question two. Why can't the body repair enamel that has been lost?
Answer. Enamel contains no living cells.
Question three. Why can you still swallow food while upside down?
Answer. Muscle waves push food along the tube.
Question four. What does the 2016 recount of microbial and human cells show?
Answer. Catchy statistics can outlive their evidence.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
